evidence.text:
Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

gold.abstract: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are an established technique to screen for abnormal cardiac signals. Recent work has established that it is possible to detect arrhythmia directly from the ECG signal using deep learning algorithms. While a few prior approaches with contrastive learning have been successful, the best way to define a positive sample remains an open question. In this project, we investigate several ways to define positive samples, and assess which approach yields the best performance in a downstream task of classifying arrhythmia. We explore spatiotemporal invariances, generic augmentations, demographic similarities, cardiac rhythms, and wave attributes of ECG as potential ways to match positive samples. We then evaluate each strategy with downstream task performance, and find that learned representations invariant to patient identity are powerful in arrhythmia detection. We made our code available in: https://github.com/mandiehyewon/goodviews_ecg.git

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- [paper-c] provides an AI-enabled ECG model (convolutional neural network) trained on paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data (n=44,959) to detect asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD, ejection fraction ≤35%). It yields AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7% on 52,870 independent patients, and predicts future ventricular dysfunction (HR 4.1). Contribution: a validated, low-cost screening tool mapping ECG waveforms to contractile dysfunction risk.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
The ECG model outputs a continuous risk score (probability of ALVD) from raw waveform morphology. This score can serve as a physiological proxy for subclinical myocardial stress. The proposed integration links this score to **behavioral intervention targeting**: because the model identifies asymptomatic individuals at elevated risk, it creates a causal pathway for testing whether **personalized risk feedback** (derived from the AI-ECG score) modifies patient health behaviors (e.g., medication adherence, physical activity) and downstream cardiac outcomes. The mechanism is operational: the AI score becomes the exposure variable in a randomized trial of risk communication.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
- **Population**: 600 asymptomatic primary-care patients aged 50–75 with no known heart failure, randomized 1:1.
- **Intervention**: All receive a 12-lead ECG. Intervention arm receives a personalized “AI-ECG cardiac risk report” (score category: low/moderate/high) plus standard lifestyle advice; control receives standard advice only.
- **Measurements**: Primary outcome: change in daily step count (wearable) and self-reported medication adherence at 6 months. Secondary: repeat ECG at 12 months to compute change in AI-ECG risk score; incident ALVD on echocardiogram.
- **Validation**: AI-ECG score recalibrated on local cohort (n=200) against echocardiographic ejection fraction; test-retest reliability of score over 2 weeks.
- **Analysis**: ANCOVA for behavior change; Cox regression for incident ALVD.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose to test whether an AI-enabled ECG screening score for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction can be repurposed as a behavioral activation tool. Building on a validated convolutional neural network that maps ECG waveforms to contractile dysfunction risk, we will randomize asymptomatic primary-care patients to receive either personalized AI-ECG risk feedback or standard care. Our hypothesis is that feedback will increase physical activity and medication adherence, thereby reducing the AI-ECG risk score over 12 months and lowering incident dysfunction. This would transform a diagnostic screening tool into a preventive intervention, extending its clinical utility beyond detection.

FINAL IDEA: Use the AI-ECG risk score for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction as a personalized feedback mechanism to causally test whether risk communication improves health behaviors and reduces future cardiac dysfunction.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper A contributes a concrete method: using wearable physiological sensors (EDA, HRV) to continuously measure stress in field settings, with validated algorithms for stress episode detection. Paper B contributes a theory: social identity complexity (overlapping group memberships) buffers intergroup anxiety and improves perspective-taking in diverse teams.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Hypothesized causal chain: higher social identity complexity in a diverse team reduces intergroup anxiety (from Paper B), which lowers physiological stress reactivity during collaborative tasks (measurable via Paper A’s method). The mechanism is that overlapping identities provide cognitive resources for reappraising intergroup contact as non-threatening, thereby dampening autonomic arousal.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Recruit 60 diverse student teams (mixed ethnicity, gender, discipline). Measure each member’s social identity complexity via a validated questionnaire (Paper B). Teams perform a 45-minute collaborative design task while wearing wristbands (Empatica E4) that record EDA and HRV (Paper A). Apply Paper A’s stress-episode detection algorithm to derive per-person stress reactivity scores. After the task, measure intergroup anxiety using Paper B’s scale. Statistical mediation model: social identity complexity → intergroup anxiety → physiological stress reactivity, controlling for baseline arousal, personality, and team familiarity. Validate by comparing high- vs. low-complexity teams on stress episode frequency and self-reported anxiety.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
This project tests whether social identity complexity reduces physiological stress in diverse teams by lowering intergroup anxiety. Using wearable sensors and validated stress detection, we examine a causal pathway linking cognitive identity structures to autonomic responses during real collaboration. The contribution beyond either paper is a mechanistic, psychophysiological account of how identity complexity “gets under the skin” in diverse teamwork, enabling future interventions that target identity structures to reduce stress-related conflict.

FINAL IDEA: Social identity complexity lowers intergroup anxiety, which in turn reduces physiological stress reactivity during diverse teamwork, testable via wearable stress detection and mediation analysis.
